arXiv:2507.10287v1 [quant-ph] 14 Jul 2025

Grassmann Variational Monte Carlo with neural wave functions

Douglas Hendry Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland    Alessandro Sinibaldi Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland    Giuseppe Carleo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract

Excited states play a central role in determining the physical properties of quantum matter, yet their accurate computation in many-body systems remains a formidable challenge for numerical methods. While neural quantum states have delivered outstanding results for ground-state problems, extending their applicability to excited states has faced limitations, including instability in dense spectra and reliance on symmetry constraints or penalty-based formulations. In this work, we rigorously formalize the framework introduced by Pfau et al. [1] in terms of Grassmann geometry of the Hilbert space. This allows us to generalize the Stochastic Reconfiguration method for the simultaneous optimization of multiple variational wave functions, and to introduce the multidimensional versions of operator variances and overlaps. We validate our approach on the Heisenberg quantum spin model on the square lattice, achieving highly accurate energies and physical observables for a large number of excited states.

I Introduction

Quantum matter does not reveal its full character in the ground state. Optical spectra, thermodynamic response, and non-equilibrium dynamics are all controlled by the excited spectrum. The exact computation of low-lying excited states suffers from the curse of dimensionality of quantum many-body Hilbert spaces, limiting exact calculations to a few particles. For ab-initio problems, equation-of-motion coupled-cluster (EOM-CC) reduces the prefactor but not the exponential wall [2]. Quantum Monte Carlo helps in certain models, yet the sign problem usually comes back where correlations are strongest [3]. Tensor networks (TN) go furthest in one dimension: the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) gives almost exact spectra for gapped chains [4]. In two and three dimensions — or in frustrated lattices — the relevant excitations carry more entanglement; higher-dimensional TN, such as PEPS [5] and MERA [6], treat only small clusters before the cost again balloons with system width and bond dimension. Accurate excited-state calculations for higher-dimensional or frustrated quantum Hamiltonians, therefore, remain an open challenge.

Since their introduction, neural quantum states (NQS) [7] have provided several state-of-the-art results for ground state search, including spin [8, 9, 10, 11], bosonic [12] and electronic models [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], as well as competitive performance in simulating quantum many-body dynamics [18, 19, 20, 21]. Extending that success to excited states is challenging. Early NQS schemes enforced point-group or momentum quantum numbers [22] but could only target a single eigenvector at a time. Penalty-based and folded-spectrum approaches [23, 24] introduce auxiliary cost terms in the variational problem to discourage collapse into the ground state, at the price of complicated hyperparameter tuning and increased variance. Recently, Pfau et al. [1] reformulated the excitation search as a ground-state problem of an enlarged Hamiltonian, eliminating the need for imposing symmetries and orthogonalization.

In this work, we rigorously generalize the framework of Ref. [1] by formulating it in geometric terms, making use of the Grassmann structure inherent in the Hilbert space. This method avoids to invert the possibly ill-conditioned Gram matrix of the basis states, which plays the role of a multidimensional normalization factor. As such, it provides a natural extension of standard Variational Monte Carlo [25] to the concurrent optimization of multiple quantum states. In particular, we generalize the Stochastic Reconfiguration [26] method to optimize several variational wave functions simultaneously, and we introduce multidimensional formulations of operator variances and overlaps. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it in second quantization on the 2D Heisenberg quantum spin model, achieving remarkable accuracy in both the energy and the spin structure factor for a substantial number of excited states.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the various representations of linear subspaces within the Hilbert space. Section 3 extends the definitions of expectation value, variance, and overlap to Grassmannians. Section 4 formalizes the variational geometry of linear subspaces and presents the Grassmann Variational Monte Carlo method. Section 5 describes the neural network architecture employed and presents numerical results for the two-dimensional Heisenberg model. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and discusses directions for future research.

II Representations of Linear Subspaces

II.1 Basis Representation

We consider a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}. The space comprising all possible NN-dimensional linear subspaces 𝒱\mathcal{V} of ℋ\mathcal{H} forms a differential manifold which is the Grassmannian 𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}). One of the most interesting and studied aspects of Grassmann manifolds is the multitude of ways they can be parameterized and embedded in other spaces.

The most straightforward way to parametrize a linear subspace is through a chosen basis. We define a linear subspace 𝒱∈𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathcal{V}\in\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) in terms of a given set of basis states {ϕ1,…,ϕN}\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\} as the “basis representation”. This representation will serve as our primary reference point from which all the other representations presented will be defined in relation. To facilitate this, it is convenient to consider ordered bases. We denote a particular ordered basis, and more generally any collection of individual states, with a capital letter and the individual states with the indexed lowercase as

Φ=(ϕ1,…,ϕN)∈ℋ⊗N.\Phi=(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})\in\mathcal{H}^{\otimes N}. (1)

For each basis Φ\Phi, its Gram matrix, denoted as G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi), is the N×NN\times N overlap matrix between the basis pairs. Its dual basis, denoted as Φ~\widetilde{\Phi}, is the equivalent basis such that the relative overlaps are given as ⟨ϕ~i|ϕj⟩=δi​j\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{i}|\phi_{j}\rangle=\delta_{ij}.

II.2 Matrix Representation

The matrix representation is an alternative representation of a linear subspace, which is more suitable for working with Grassmannians. We start by introducing the matrix analog of the bra-ket inner product. This corresponds to the overlap matrix of two tuples of states Φ=(ϕ1,…,ϕN)\Phi=(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}) and Ψ=(ψ1,…,ψN)\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{N}) which is expressed as the overlap between the “bra matrix” [[Ψ|\lbb\Psi| and the “ket matrix” |Φ]]|\Phi\rbb:

[[⁡Ψ|Φ​]]=[⟨ψ1|ϕ1⟩…⟨ψ1|ϕN⟩⋱⟨ψN|ϕ1⟩…⟨ψN|ϕN⟩].\lbb\Psi|\Phi\rbb=\begin{bmatrix}\langle\psi_{1}|\phi_{1}\rangle&\dots&\langle\psi_{1}|\phi_{N}\rangle\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \langle\psi_{N}|\phi_{1}\rangle&\ldots&\langle\psi_{N}|\phi_{N}\rangle\end{bmatrix}. (2)

The row vectors of the N×|ℋ|N\times|\mathcal{H}| bra matrix [[Ψ|\lbb\Psi| and the column vectors of the |ℋ|×N|\mathcal{H}|\times N ket matrix |Φ]]|\Phi\rbb are given by the ordered bras of Ψ\Psi and kets of Φ\Phi respectively. The N×NN\times N overlap matrix [[⁡Ψ|Φ​]]\lbb\Psi|\Phi\rbb is given by all the ordered overlaps between the basis states.

For a linear subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the equations for their bases can be expressed compactly in this matrix representation. For a basis Φ\Phi, the Gram matrix is then G=[[⁡Φ|Φ​]]G=\lbb\Phi|\Phi\rbb and the the bra matrix of its dual basis Φ~\widetilde{\Phi} is given by the pseudo inverse of the basis ket matrix [[Φ~|=(|Φ]])(+)=G−1[[Φ|\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|=\left(|\Phi\rbb\right)^{(+)}=G^{-1}\lbb\Phi|. Changes of basis can be expressed in terms of matrix multiplications for any non-singular matrix X∈G​LN​(ℂ)X\in GL_{N}(\mathbb{C}) as |Φ]]→|Φ]]⋅X|\Phi\rbb\rightarrow|\Phi\rbb\cdot X and [[Φ~|→X−1⋅[[Φ~|\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\rightarrow X^{-1}\cdot\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}| for the corresponding dual basis. The equivalent basis representation of the Grassmann manifold 𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) can now be recast in the matrix representation as the orbits/equivalence classes of full rank ket matrices with respect to group action on the right by G​LN​(ℂ)GL_{N}(\mathbb{C}) [27].

II.3 Wedge Product Representation

Another useful representation for Grassmannians, the so-called wedge product representation, is generated by the Plücker embedding 𝐆𝐫N(ℋ)→𝐏(∧Nℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H})\rightarrow\mathbf{P}(\wedge^{N}\mathcal{H}), where ∧\wedge denotes the wedge product. This allows each linear subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V} to be represented uniquely (up to an overall constant) as a single wave-function in the expanded anti-symmetric Hilbert space ∧Nℋ\wedge^{N}\mathcal{H}. This provides a blueprint for formulating the Grassmann version of Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) as a standard single state VMC in ∧Nℋ\wedge^{N}\mathcal{H}, as done by Pfau et al. [1]. Considering a basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the single state representation of 𝒱\mathcal{V} is given by the wedge product of the individual basis states as

|Φ⟩⟩∧=⋀i=1N|ϕi⟩=∑σ∈{perms}sgn(σ)|ϕOPENσ⁡(1))⟩|ϕσ⁡(2)⟩…,|\Phi\rwa=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{N}|\phi_{i}\rangle=\sum_{\sigma\in\{\text{perms}\}}\text{sgn}(\sigma)\,|\phi_{\sigma{(1)})}\rangle|\phi_{\sigma{(2)}}\rangle\ldots, (3)

where the sum runs over all the possible permutations of the indices. We will refer to the previous representation as the “wedge product representation” of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Changes of basis in the matrix representation |Φ]]→|Φ]]⋅X|\Phi\rbb\rightarrow|\Phi\rbb\cdot X translate into the wedge product representation as |Φ⟩⟩→det⁡(X)⋅|Φ⟩⟩|\Phi\rangle\!\rangle\rightarrow\det(X)\cdot|\Phi\rangle\!\rangle. This ensures that all the wedge products of equivalent bases lie in the same ray of the projective space 𝐏(∧Nℋ)\mathbf{P}(\wedge^{N}\mathcal{H}). The bras ⟨⟨Φ|\lwa\Phi|, from the wedge product of the individual state bras, are normalized by a factor of 1/N!1/N!. Then, the wedge product overlaps relate to the corresponding overlap matrices as the determinants, namely:

⟨⟨⁡Ψ|Φ​⟩⟩∧=det​([[Ψ|Φ]]).\lwa\Psi|\Phi\rwa=\text{det}\left(\,[\![\Psi|\Phi]\!]\,\right). (4)

II.4 Projector and Density Operator Representations

Every linear subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V} has a unique operator representation as the orthogonal projector P^𝒱:ℋ→𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}, of which projects the full Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} onto itself. In terms of the orthogonal eigenstates, P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}} is defined so that the NN eigenstates of eigenvalue one collectively span 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The remaining eigenstates, all of eigenvalue zero, then collectively span 𝒱⟂\mathcal{V}^{\perp} as the set of states that are orthogonal to all the states in 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The orthogonal projector for 𝒱⟂\mathcal{V}^{\perp} is then the complementary projector P^𝒱⟂=1−P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}=1-\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}, which equivalently projects out of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The orthogonal projector P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}} can be constructed from any basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the sum of the outer products of each basis and dual basis pair. In the matrix representation, this corresponds simply to the basis ket matrix times the dual basis bra matrix:

P^𝒱=∑k=1N|ϕk⟩​⟨ϕ~k|=|Φ​]]⁡[[⁡Φ~|.\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}|\phi_{k}\rangle\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{k}|=|\Phi\rbb\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|. (5)

The dimension of any linear subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V} can be expressed algebraically as the trace of its orthogonal projector P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}. Each Grassmannian 𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) can then be expressed bijectively as the set of the orthogonal projectors whose traces equal NN. Additionally, by rescaling an orthogonal projector P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}} by the constant factor 1/N1/N, it becomes a density operator. This then gives an equivalent “density operator representation” for each linear subspace 𝒱∈𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathcal{V}\in\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}):

ρ^𝒱=1N​P^𝒱.\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}}=\frac{1}{N}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}. (6)

The density operator ρ^𝒱\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}} for each 𝒱\mathcal{V} can be defined directly so that its support is 𝒱\mathcal{V} and its weighting of states in 𝒱\mathcal{V} is uniform. This equivalent representation will provide another perspective for quantum applications. In the following sections, when attempting to extend quantum definitions to linear subspaces 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the proposed quantities can be formulated from the mixed state definitions for ρ^𝒱\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}}.

III Quantum Grassmannians

III.1 Extending Quantum Definitions to Linear Subspaces

The term quantum Grassmannian can be found elsewhere in the literature with very different definitions. However, we will use it to refer generally to the extension of quantum concepts to Grassmannians. The central idea is to generalize standard quantum definitions — typically formulated for rays as the unique representations of physical states — to linear subspaces in the Hilbert space. As the projective Hilbert space P⁡(ℋ)P(\mathcal{H}) is the Grassmannian 𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) for N=1N=1, this extension is quite natural and much of the work in Grassmann geometry is rooted in this perspective as an extension of projective geometry.

Though in theory all or most aspects of quantum mechanics could be extended to Grassmannians, in this work we will be concerned only with the extension of basic quantum values such as operator expectation, variance, overlap/fidelity, and their practical numerical applications to standard quantum problems. The Grassmann extension for a quantum value is given essentially by promoting the scalar value to a basis-dependent N×NN\times N matrix, whose basis-independent eigenvalues form a set of NN individual quantum values or similarly defined values. These Grassmann matrix analogs for scalar quantum values arise across a broad range of contexts.

III.1.1 Promoting Scalars to Matrices

The promotion of scalars to matrices is formulated functionally, such that a defined quantum value as scalar mapping of states ϕ→f⁡(ϕ)\phi\rightarrow f(\phi) is extended to analogous matrix mapping of bases Φ→F⁡(Φ)\Phi\rightarrow F(\Phi). The scalar mapping of states, which inherently is a mapping of rays, is invariant under multiplication by a constant |ϕ⟩→x​|ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle\rightarrow x|\phi\rangle to ensure the same value for all the states in the same ray. This translates for bases, as representations of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, to equivariance of the matrix mapping for changes of equivalent basis. To ensure the eigenvalues are inherent to 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the equivariance takes the form of similarity transformations, so that |Φ]]→|Φ]]⋅X|\Phi\rbb\rightarrow|\Phi\rbb\cdot X results in F→X−1⋅F⋅XF\rightarrow X^{-1}\cdot F\cdot X.

The exact form of the matrix promotion F⁡(Φ)F(\Phi) of any given scalar quantum value f⁡(ϕ)f(\phi) can be derived by following the same general set of procedures. This is because any relevant quantum value is formed functionally as the composite of some algebraically simple function of a set of overlaps between pairs of states or with an operator in between. Firstly, each of the composite overlaps is promoted to an N×NN\times N overlap matrix by replacing the single state bras and kets of ϕ\phi with the bra and ket matrices respectively of Φ\Phi. By plugging the overlap matrices into the overlap function, algebraic scalar multiplication and division become matrix multiplication and multiplication by matrix inverse respectively. Due to the non-commutativity of matrix multiplications, this leaves multiple definitions for each possible ordering of the matrices. Finally, the correct ordering is identified as the one that ensures the desired equivariance under similarity transformations.

III.1.2 Principal Values and Bases

The construction of the matrix analog for a given quantum value ensures that the matrix eigenvalues are a set of NN corresponding quantum values, which we will refer to as the “principal values”. Each principal value λi\lambda_{i} is the given quantum value or a similarly defined value for a corresponding state ui∈𝒱u_{i}\in\mathcal{V}. Collectively, these corresponding “principal states” UU are always constrained to be linearly independent and thus form a unique (up to individual constants) “principal basis.” The principal basis UU is determined as the basis that diagonalizes the matrices as F⁡(U)=ΛF(U)=\Lambda. Practically, the principal values and the basis can be obtained from any basis Φ\Phi by an eigendecomposition F⁡(Φ)=X⋅Λ⋅X−1F(\Phi)=X\cdot\Lambda\cdot X^{-1}, where the eigenvector matrix XX provides the change of basis |U]]=|Φ]]⋅X|U\rbb=|\Phi\rbb\cdot X.

The Grassmann extension of a given quantum value can now be expressed properly in terms of linear subspaces and independently of their basis representations. Fundamentally, the single quantum value for rays is extended to a set of NN quantum values for linear subspaces, given by the principal values. As an additional component, the given quantum value also selects a unique basis for each linear subspace, given by the principal basis.

III.2 Operators

III.2.1 Operator Expectation Matrices

We will refer to the matrix promotion of a pure state operator expectation value as an operator expectation matrix (OEM). For a Hermitian operator A^\hat{A} and a basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the OEM A~​(Φ)\widetilde{A}(\Phi) is given by the operator overlap matrix A⁡(Φ)=[[⁡Φ​|A^|​Φ​]]A(\Phi)=\lbb\Phi|\hat{A}|\Phi\rbb normalized on the left by the inverse of the Gram matrix, namely A~​(Φ)=G−1​(Φ)⋅A⁡(Φ)\widetilde{A}(\Phi)=G^{-1}(\Phi)\cdot A(\Phi). The normalization equivalently transforms the basis bras into dual basis bras. The OEM A~​(Φ)\widetilde{A}(\Phi) is thus the operator overlap matrix for mixed dual basis bra and basis ket pairs:

A~​(Φ)=[[Φ~​|A^|​Φ]]=[⟨ϕ~1|A^|ϕ1⟩…⟨ϕ~1|A^|ϕN⟩⋱⟨ϕ~N|A^|ϕ1⟩…⟨ϕ~N|A^|ϕN⟩].\widetilde{A}(\Phi)=[\![\widetilde{\Phi}|\hat{A}|\Phi]\!]=\begin{bmatrix}\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{1}|\hat{A}|\phi_{1}\rangle&\dots&\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{1}|\hat{A}|\phi_{N}\rangle\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \langle\widetilde{\phi}_{N}|\hat{A}|\phi_{1}\rangle&\ldots&\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{N}|\hat{A}|\phi_{N}\rangle\end{bmatrix}. (7)

The OEMs of A^\hat{A} for all the bases of 𝒱\mathcal{V} encode all the pure state expectation values for every state in 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Transforming to any orthogonal basis |Φ]]→|Φ]]⋅X|\Phi\rbb\rightarrow|\Phi\rbb\cdot X with A~→X−1⋅A~⋅X\widetilde{A}\rightarrow X^{-1}\cdot\widetilde{A}\cdot X, the diagonal matrix elements give each individual ⟨A^⟩ϕi≡⟨ϕi|​A^​|ϕi⟩/⟨ϕi|​|ϕi⟩\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\phi_{i}}\equiv\bra{\phi_i}\hat{A}\ket{\phi_i}/\bra{\phi_i}\ket{\phi_i}. The principal operator expectation basis UU is then the basis for which all the off-diagonal entries are zero. The principal operator expectation values {λi}\{\lambda_{i}\}, as the OEM eigenvalues for every basis of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, are each individually the pure state expectations λi=⟨A^⟩ui\lambda_{i}=\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{u_{i}}.

The OEMs and the importance of the principal values and basis can be understood in terms of operator projections. An operator A^\hat{A} acting on the full Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} is projected to an operator acting only on 𝒱⊂ℋ\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{H} as A^𝒱=P^𝒱​A^​P^𝒱\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}}=\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}. Expressed in terms of any basis Φ\Phi, the matrix elements of the projected operator A^𝒱\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}} are then given by the OEM A~​(Φ)\widetilde{A}(\Phi). As the principal basis OEM is diagonal A~​(U)=Λ\widetilde{A}(U)=\Lambda, they form the eigenstates of A^𝒱\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}} and the principal values are the eigenvalues. Therefore, we can write:

A^𝒱\displaystyle\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}} =|Φ​]]⋅A~​(Φ)⋅[[⁡Φ~|=∑ijA~ij​(Φ)​|ϕi⟩​⟨ϕ~j|\displaystyle=|\Phi\rbb\cdot\widetilde{A}(\Phi)\cdot\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|=\sum_{ij}\widetilde{A}_{ij}(\Phi)\,|\phi_{i}\rangle\langle\widetilde{\phi}_{j}| (8)
=|U​]]⋅A~​(U)⋅[[⁡U~|=∑kλk​|uk⟩​⟨u~k|.\displaystyle=|U\rbb\cdot\widetilde{A}(U)\cdot\lbb\widetilde{U}|=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\,|u_{k}\rangle\langle\widetilde{u}_{k}|.

As the eigenstates of A^𝒱\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}}, the uniqueness (up to overall constants) of UU is guaranteed only if the principal values/eigenvalues are not degenerate. Importantly, these degrees of freedom for UU correspond directly with the degrees for XX from eigendecomposition A~​(Φ)=X⋅Λ⋅X−1\widetilde{A}(\Phi)=X\cdot\Lambda\cdot X^{-1}. When obtained as |U]]=|Φ]]⋅X|U\rbb=|\Phi\rbb\cdot X, the orthogonality is guaranteed only for the nondegenerate case.

The determination of the principal values and basis can be viewed as finding the set of NN closest approximate eigenvalues λi\lambda_{i} and eigenstates |ui⟩|u_{i}\rangle of A^\hat{A}, constrained so that span⁡(U)=𝒱\spn(U)=\mathcal{V}. As the exact eigenvalue and eigenstate pairs of the projected operator A^𝒱\hat{A}_{\mathcal{V}}, the approximation is given so that each residual error |ri⟩=(A^−λi)​|ui⟩|r_{i}\rangle=(\hat{A}-\lambda_{i})|u_{i}\rangle is orthogonal to 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

III.2.2 Operator Variance and Covariance Matrices

The corresponding operator variance matrices (OVMs) as the promotions of pure state operator variances are formed as matrix analogs of their scalar counterparts. For a Hermitian operator A^\hat{A} and basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the OVM corresponds to Σ~(A)​(Φ)=A~(2)​(Φ)−A~2​(Φ)\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(A)}(\Phi)=\widetilde{A}^{(2)}(\Phi)-\widetilde{A}^{2}(\Phi), where A~(2)\widetilde{A}^{(2)} denotes the OEM for A^2\hat{A}^{2} and A~2=A~⋅A~\widetilde{A}^{2}=\widetilde{A}\cdot\widetilde{A}. Just as the pure state operator variance for a state ϕ\phi can be expressed equivalently as operator expectation of A^​P^ϕ⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\phi^{\perp}}\hat{A}, the OVM can be expressed equivalently as the OEM of A^​P^𝒱⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A}. The projector P^ϕ⟂\hat{P}_{\phi^{\perp}}, which projects out the single state ϕ\phi, is promoted to P^𝒱⟂\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}} ,which projects out all the states in 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Operator covariance matrices (OCMs) for two operators A^\hat{A} and B^\hat{B} , which we denote as Σ~(A​B)​(Φ)\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(AB)}(\Phi), are formulated similarly. Hence, we have:

Σ~(A)​(Φ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(A)}(\Phi) =A~(2)​(Φ)−A~2​(Φ)=[[⁡Φ~​|A^​P^𝒱⟂​A^|​Φ​]],\displaystyle=\widetilde{A}^{(2)}(\Phi)-\widetilde{A}^{2}(\Phi)=\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A}|\Phi\rbb, (9)
Σ~(A​B)​(Φ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(AB)}(\Phi) =A​B~​(Φ)−A~​(Φ)⋅B~​(Φ)=[[⁡Φ~​|A^​P^𝒱⟂​B^|​Φ​]].\displaystyle=\widetilde{AB}(\Phi)-\widetilde{A}(\Phi)\cdot\widetilde{B}(\Phi)=\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{B}|\Phi\rbb.

As the OVM of A^\hat{A} is the OEM of A^​P^𝒱⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A}, the principal operator variances {σk2}\{\sigma_{k}^{2}\} are not the exact pure state variances of the principal basis WW. As for each wkw_{k}, σk2\sigma_{k}^{2} and Varwk⁡[A^]≡⟨A^2⟩wk−⟨A^⟩wk2\Var_{w_{k}}[\hat{A}]\equiv\langle\hat{A}^{2}\rangle_{w_{k}}-\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{w_{k}}^{2} are given by the expectation values of A^​P^𝒱⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A} and A^​P^wk⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{w_{k}^{\perp}}\hat{A} respectively. As P^𝒱⟂\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}} projects out wkw_{k}, as well as the the other states, the two variances are in general not equal but bounded as 0≤σi2≤Varwi⁡[A^]0\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq\Var_{w_{i}}[\hat{A}]. The principal operator covariances are then the expectations of A^​P^𝒱⟂​B^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{B} and are similarly bounded in absolute value with the pure state operator covariances.

The modified variances as expectations of A^​P^𝒱⟂​A^\hat{A}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A} can be obtained individually for any orthogonal basis from the OVM diagonals. Importantly, unique to the principal operator expectation basis UU, these all equate exactly to the pure state operator variances:

Σ~i​i(A)​(U)=Varui⁡[A^].\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(A)}_{ii}(U)=\Var_{u_{i}}[\hat{A}]. (10)

From the previous section, each operator image given as A^​|ui⟩=λi​|ui⟩+⟂𝒱\hat{A}|u_{i}\rangle=\lambda_{i}|u_{i}\rangle+\perp\mathcal{V} is already orthogonal to all the other states uju_{j}. Thus, the subsequent projections by either P^𝒱⟂\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}} or P^ui⟂\hat{P}_{u_{i}^{\perp}} are equivalent.

The OVMs can also be understood geometrically as encoding information about how much of the operator image space A^​𝒱\hat{A}\mathcal{V} lies outside of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. This corresponds to the residual space ℛ⟂𝒱\mathcal{R}\perp\mathcal{V}, given so that A^​𝒱⊂𝒱+ℛ\hat{A}\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{V}+\mathcal{R}. For any basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, a corresponding residual basis of ℛ\mathcal{R} can be obtained as |R]]=P^𝒱⟂A^|Φ]]|R\rbb=\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{A}|\Phi\rbb. For orthonormal bases, the OVMs Σ~(A)​(Φ)\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(A)}(\Phi) then reduce to their Gram matrix G⁡(R)G(R). The modified operator variances from the diagonals, then, equate to their norms ‖ri‖2|\!|r_{i}|\!|^{2} as a set of individual measures relative to the scalings of A^\hat{A}. The principal operator variance basis can thus be defined equivalently as the unique orthogonal basis whose residual basis is also orthogonal. Together, these give respectively the ideal bases for relating 𝒱\mathcal{V} and ℛ\mathcal{R} with one another.

III.2.3 Monte Carlo Estimations of Operator Matrices

The standard variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method for estimating operator values for a single quantum state can be extended to the estimations of their matrix promotions using the same Grassmann formulation, which we will refer to as Grassmann variational Monte Carlo (GVMC). Fig. 1 shows a table of comparison between VMC and GVMC. The fundamentals of GVMC, originally developed by Pfau et al. [1], are a “determinant sampling scheme” and a corresponding promotion of the local operator values to matrices. Together, OEMs can then be estimated directly, like in standard VMC, as the average of the local operator matrices. In this section, we show that OVMs and OCMs can also be estimated similarly, as an extension of standard VMC. In a later section, we will show that the same can be done for the estimations of the overlap and the fidelity.

For an orthonormal basis |s⟩{\ket{s}} of the Hilbert space, the determinant sampling scheme [1] involves drawing configurations in batches, such that a single sample corresponds to a NN-tuple of basis states S=(s1,…,sN)S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}). These are drawn from the distribution of the wedge product representation PΦ​(S)∝|⟨⟨⁡S​|Φ​⟩⟩∧|2P_{\Phi}(S)\propto|\lwa S|\Phi\rwa|^{2} as in standard VMC. In the matrix representation, the scalar wavefunction coefficients ϕ⁡(s)=⟨s|ϕ⟩\phi(s)=\langle s|\phi\rangle become the N×NN\times N overlap matrices Φ⁡(S)=[[⁡S|Φ​]]\Phi(S)=\lbb S|\Phi\rbb and from Eq. 4 the wedge product coefficients are their determinants ⟨⟨⁡S|Φ​⟩⟩∧=det⁡[Φ⁡(S)]\lwa S|\Phi\rwa=\det[\Phi(S)]. Conveniently, including all the N!N! orderings of the individual states, the probability of each NN-tuple SS is then

PΦ​(S)=|det⁡(Φ⁡(S))|2N!​det⁡[G⁡(Φ)].P_{\Phi}(S)=\frac{|\det(\Phi(S))|^{2}}{N!\det[G(\Phi)]}. (11)

The probabilities are invariant under changes of equivalent bases and thus each SS is weighted with respect to 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

The determinant sampling allows the expectation value matrix A~\widetilde{A} to be estimated directly as the Monte Carlo average of the local operator matrix A~​(S)\widetilde{A}(S) [1]:

A~​(Φ)=𝔼S∼PΦ​[A~​(S)].\widetilde{A}(\Phi)=\mathbb{E}_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}[\widetilde{A}(S)]. (12)

For each sampled state tuple SS, the local operator matrix A~​(S)\widetilde{A}(S) is constructed as a matrix extension of the standard scalar local operator values. The operator overlap matrix A⁡(S)=[[⁡S​|A^|​Φ​]]A(S)=\lbb S|\hat{A}|\Phi\rbb is normalized by the inverse of the overlap matrix Φ⁡(S)=[[⁡S|Φ​]]\Phi(S)=\lbb S|\Phi\rbb such that:

A~​(S)=Φ−1​(S)⋅A⁡(S).\widetilde{A}(S)=\Phi^{-1}(S)\cdot A(S). (13)

Importantly, this bypasses the need for separate estimations of the unnormalized expectation value matrix A=[[⁡Φ|A^​Φ​]]A=\lbb\Phi|\hat{A}\Phi\rbb and the Gram matrix GG, as well as its inversion which can be unstable with finite samples.

We now introduce a way of obtaining OVMs and OCMs using the same determinant sampling of local operator matrices. The matrix extension of this, as dictated by the determinant sampling, becomes the covariance matrix of the trace of one local operator matrix with the individual matrix elements of the other:

Σ~i​j(A)​(Φ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}_{ij}^{(A)}(\Phi) =CovS∼PΦ⁡[Tr⁡(A~​(S)),A~ij​(S)],\displaystyle=\Cov_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\Tr(\widetilde{A}(S) ),\widetilde{A}_{ij}(S)\right], (14)
Σ~i​j(A​B)​(Φ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}_{ij}^{(AB)}(\Phi) =CovS∼PΦ⁡[Tr⁡(A~​(S)),B~ij​(S)].\displaystyle=\Cov_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\Tr(\widetilde{A}(S) ),\widetilde{B}_{ij}(S)\right].

This asymmetric formulation between the local operator matrices is a consequence of the normalization by the Gram matrix inverse on the left. The full covariance between the local operator matrices 𝔼S∼PΦ⁡[A~†​(S)⊗B~​(S)]−𝔼S∼PΦ⁡[A~†​(S)]⊗𝔼S′∼PΦ⁡[B~​(S′)]\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}[\widetilde{A}^{\dagger}(S)\otimes\widetilde{B}(S)]-\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}[\widetilde{A}^{\dagger}(S)]\otimes\Ex_{S^{\prime}\sim P_{\Phi}}[\widetilde{B}(S^{\prime})] equates to G−1⊗Σ(A​B)G^{-1}\otimes\Sigma^{(AB)}, but with the relative indices permuted. Therefore, the contractions that give Σ~(A​B)=G−1⋅Σ(A​B)\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(AB)}=G^{-1}\cdot\Sigma^{(AB)} correspond to taking the traces of A~†​(S)\widetilde{A}^{\dagger}(S). In an orthogonal basis, the diagonal OVM or OCM matrix elements Σi​i(A​B)\Sigma_{ii}^{(AB)} can be obtained alternatively, without the contractions, from the i​i​i​iiiii tensor elements of the full covariance. This corresponds to the “variance estimator” described in [1]. As explained in the previous section, these tensor elements give the modified operator variances and covariances, which only in some cases are the individual pure state operator variances and covariances. The sampling expressions for the OEMs, OVMs, and OCMs are discussed in detail in Sections .2 and .3.

III.2.4 Scalar Grassmann Operator Values

Scalar Grassmann operator values can be defined naturally for each linear subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the arithmetic means of the principal operator values. These can then be obtained from the operator matrices as their traces normalized by 1/N1/N. Without the normalization by 1/N1/N, these are all equivalently the corresponding pure state operator values on the wedge product state |Φ⟩⟩∧|\Phi\rwa, with the operators becoming the directed sums A^→A^⊕¯​N=A^⊗I⊗…+I⊗A^⊗…+…\hat{A}\rightarrow\hat{A}^{\overline{\oplus}N}=\hat{A}\otimes I\otimes\ldots+I\otimes\hat{A}\otimes\ldots+\ldots. Additionally, taking the traces of all the GVMC expressions for the operator matrices reduces to the standard VMC expressions for |Φ⟩⟩∧|\Phi\rwa, as the traces of the local operator matrices for Φ\Phi equate to the local operator values for |Φ⟩⟩∧|\Phi\rwa. In the density operator representation, the scalar Grassmann operator expectation (with the normalization) is equal to the mixed state operator expectation for ρ^𝒱\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}}, while the scalar Grassmann operator variance and covariance give different definitions than the mixed state ones.

The Grassmann operator expectation value ⟨A^⟩𝒱=(1/N)​𝔼S∼PΦ​[Tr⁡[A~​(S)]]\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}=(1/N)\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\Tr[\widetilde{A}(S)]\right] is the average of the principal operator expectations, each of which is again the pure state expectation ⟨A^⟩ui\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{u_{i}} of the corresponding principal basis state uiu_{i}. As a loss function, ⟨A^⟩𝒱\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} corresponds to collectively minimizing all the expectation values ⟨A^⟩ui\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{u_{i}} with an orthogonality constraint ⟨ui|uj⟩∝δi​j\langle u_{i}|u_{j}\rangle\propto\delta_{ij}, which is built in from the Grassmann formulation. This is what is done in [1] to compute the low-lying excited states of a Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}. In that case, the minimization of ⟨A^⟩𝒱\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} is over a set of NN variational wave functions Φ\Phi as an arbitrary basis of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Then, the linear combinations of the states in Φ\Phi, which give the principal basis UU, form the variational approximations of the excited states.

The Grassmann operator variance Var𝒱⁡[A^]=(1/N)​VarS∼PΦ​[Tr⁡[A~​(S)]]\Var_{\mathcal{V}}[\hat{A}]=(1/N)\Var_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\Tr[\widetilde{A}(S)]\right] as a loss function can be understood by the equivalent minimal conditions.

Var𝒱⁡[A^]=0⇔(A^−λi)​|ui⟩=0​∀i⇔A^​𝒱⊂𝒱.\Var_{\mathcal{V}}[\hat{A}]=0\Leftrightarrow(\hat{A}-\lambda_{i})|u_{i}\rangle=0\,\forall\,i\Leftrightarrow\hat{A}\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{V}. (15)

The average of the principal operator variances is equal to the average of the pure state operator variances of the principal expectation basis states UU. Thus, minimizing Var𝒱⁡[A^]\Var_{\mathcal{V}}[\hat{A}] can be used similarly to collectively minimize each Varui⁡[A^]\Var_{u_{i}}[\hat{A}] with built-in orthogonality constraints. Alternatively, Var𝒱⁡[A^]\Var_{\mathcal{V}}[\hat{A}] can be used as a penalty function to enforce the closure requirement A^​𝒱⊂𝒱\hat{A}\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{V}. The mixed state operator variance of ρ^𝒱\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}} is given as a weighted spread of the eigenvalues of A^\hat{A}. This differs from the Grassmann definition for Var𝒱⁡[A^]\Var_{\mathcal{V}}[\hat{A}], which is much less dependent on the particular eigenvalues themselves. An extremal example of the difference is given for 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the span of the two extremal eigenstates of A^\hat{A}. The Grassmann variance is minimally zero as the principal expectation states are exact eigenstates, while the mixed state operator variance is maximally (12​(λmax−λmin))2\left(\frac{1}{2}(\lambda_{\text{max}}-\lambda_{\text{min}})\right)^{2}, with λmin\lambda_{\text{min}} and λmax\lambda_{\text{max}} minimal and maximal eigenvalues respectively.

III.2.5 Wedge-Product States as Free Fermion States

We remark that a linear subspace in the wedge-product representation can be interpreted as a state of NN free fermions where single particle states are replaced by many-body wave functions. Its corresponding un-normalized amplitudes are given by:

⟨⟨S|Φ⟩⟩=det⁡[[⁡S|Φ​]].\langle\langle S|\Phi\rangle\rangle=\det\lbb S|\Phi\rbb. (16)

One can then define an extended Hamiltonian in ℋ⊗¯​N\mathcal{H}^{\overline{\otimes}N} as ℍ=H^⊗I^⊗…⊗I^+I^⊗H^⊗…⊗I^+…+I^⊗I^⊗…⊗H^\mathbb{H}=\hat{H}\otimes\hat{I}\otimes\ldots\otimes\hat{I}+\hat{I}\otimes\hat{H}\otimes\ldots\otimes\hat{I}+\ldots+\hat{I}\otimes\hat{I}\otimes\ldots\otimes\hat{H}, where H^\hat{H} is the physical Hamiltonian of interest. Since ℍ\mathbb{H} is the sum of NN non-interacting terms, its eigenstates are tensor product of the eigenstates of H^\hat{H}. In particular, the ground state of ℍ\mathbb{H} with fermionic symmetry is the Slater determinant of the first NN excited states of H^\hat{H}.

III.3 Grassmann Geometry

III.3.1 Fidelity Matrices

The fidelity between two quantum states ℱ⁡(ϕ,ψ)=⟨ϕ|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩​⟨ψ|ψ⟩\mathcal{F}(\phi,\psi)=\bra{\phi}\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}\ket{\phi}/\bra{\phi}\ket{\phi}\bra{\psi}\ket{\psi} is extended to the case of two bases Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V} and Ψ\Psi of 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime} by promoting scalar overlaps to overlap matrices, following the same procedure used in the previous generalizations. The only difference is in the last step, when selecting the matrix multiplication orderings which transform equivariantly, as now the similarity transformations for both |Φ]]→|Φ]]⋅X|\Phi\rbb\rightarrow|\Phi\rbb\cdot X and |Ψ]]→|Ψ]]⋅Y|\Psi\rbb\rightarrow|\Psi\rbb\cdot Y have to be taken into account. The result of the matrix promotion is two matrices with equivalent eigenvalues, which we denote as F⁡(Φ|Ψ)F(\Phi\,|\,\Psi) and F⁡(Ψ|Φ)F(\Psi\,|\,\Phi). The total equivariance is then given individually so that F⁡(Φ|Ψ)F(\Phi|\Psi) (F⁡(Ψ|Φ)F(\Psi|\Phi)) transforms equivariantly with respect to Φ\Phi (Ψ\Psi) and invariantly with respect to Ψ\Psi (Φ\Phi).

The orderings which give these two respective combinations of equivariance and invariance are the two orderings of the normalized overlap matrices [[⁡Φ~|Ψ​]]\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\Psi\rbb and [[⁡Ψ~|Φ​]]\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb. As the orderings can be related by a similarity transformation, their eigenvalues are the same. Analogously to their scalar counterparts, the two fidelity matrices are equivalently the two OEMs of the projectors P^𝒱′\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\prime}} and P^𝒱\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}} for Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi respectively.

F⁡(Φ|Ψ)\displaystyle F(\Phi|\Psi) =[[⁡Φ~​|Ψ​]]⋅[[⁡Ψ~|​Φ​]]=P~𝒱′​(Φ),\displaystyle=\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\Psi\rbb\cdot\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb=\widetilde{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\prime}}(\Phi), 𝒱′=span⁡(Ψ)\displaystyle\mathcal{V^{\prime}}=\spn(\Psi) (17)
F⁡(Ψ|Φ)\displaystyle F(\Psi|\Phi) =[[⁡Ψ~​|Φ​]]⋅[[⁡Φ~|​Ψ​]]=P~𝒱​(Ψ),\displaystyle=\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb\cdot\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\Psi\rbb=\widetilde{P}_{\mathcal{V}}(\Psi), 𝒱=span⁡(Φ).\displaystyle\mathcal{V}=\spn(\Phi).

From their shared eigenvalues, the principal fidelities {λi2}\{\lambda_{i}^{2}\} are defined equivalently from either fidelity matrix. From the combination of equivariance and invariance, principal bases UU of 𝒱\mathcal{V} and WW of 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime} are defined so that they each diagonalize their respective fidelity matrices as F⁡(U|Ψ)=Λ2F(U|\Psi)=\Lambda^{2} and F⁡(W|Φ)=Λ2F(W|\Phi)=\Lambda^{2}. The principal fidelities and bases are then obtained from the eigendecompositions of the fidelity matrices F⁡(Φ|Ψ)=X⋅Λ2⋅X−1F(\Phi|\Psi)=X\cdot\Lambda^{2}\cdot X^{-1} and F⁡(Ψ|Φ)=Y⋅Λ2⋅Y−1F(\Psi|\Phi)=Y\cdot\Lambda^{2}\cdot Y^{-1} with |U]]=|Φ]]⋅X|U\rbb=|\Phi\rbb\cdot X and |W]]=|Ψ]]⋅Y|W\rbb=|\Psi\rbb\cdot Y.

The principal fidelities are the exact pure state fidelities of the principal bases pairs λi2=ℱ⁡(ui,wi)\lambda_{i}^{2}=\mathcal{F}(u_{i},w_{i}). The corresponding Fubini-Study angles αi=cos−1⁡(λi)\alpha_{i}=\cos^{-1}(\lambda_{i}) give the set of Grassmann principal angles, also known as the angles between flats. These are the fundamental set of angles between 𝒱\mathcal{V} and 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime} as hyperplanes. The principal bases UU and WW, which give the corresponding direction pairs of these angles, form the ideal orthogonal bases for 𝒱\mathcal{V} and 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime} respectively for relating the two spaces to each other. Algebraically, this is formulated as UU and WW are the orthogonal bases whose mutual overlaps are ⟨ui|wj⟩∝δi​j\langle u_{i}|w_{j}\rangle\propto\delta_{ij}, which is ensured by the respective diagonalization of the fidelity matrices. Scaled as orthonormal bases with the right chosen relative phases, both overlap matrices can be expressed as [[⁡U|W​]]=[[⁡W|U​]]=Λ\lbb U|W\rbb=\lbb W|U\rbb=\Lambda. The states of WW can then be expressed in terms of UU as |wi⟩=cos⁡(αi)⁡|ui⟩+sin⁡(αi)⁡|ri⟩|w_{i}\rangle=\cos(\alpha_i)|u_{i}\rangle+\sin(\alpha_i)|r_{i}\rangle, where the states |ri⟩∝P^𝒱⟂​|wi⟩|r_{i}\rangle\propto\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|w_{i}\rangle are normalized as an orthonormal basis for the residual space ℛ⟂𝒱\mathcal{R}\perp\mathcal{V} which gives 𝒱′⊂𝒱+ℛ\mathcal{V}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{V}+\mathcal{R}.

III.3.2 Monte Carlo Estimations of Overlap and Fidelity Matrices

Here we introduce a VMC method for estimating normalized overlap and fidelity matrices. Like for operator value matrices, we use the same determinant sampling scheme Eq. 11 and formulate the sampling expressions as matrix extension of the standard VMC expressions.

For single state pairs ϕ\phi and ψ\psi, sampled in terms of ϕ\phi, the local values are given by the coefficient ratios r⁡(s)=ψ⁡(s)/ϕ⁡(s)r(s)=\psi(s)/\phi(s). Now for bases Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi, sampled in terms of Φ\Phi, the local matrices are R⁡(S)=Φ−1​(S)⋅Ψ⁡(S)R(S)=\Phi^{-1}(S)\cdot\Psi(S). The normalized overlap matrix [[⁡Φ~|Ψ​]]\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\Psi\rbb is given analogously to ⟨ϕ|ψ⟩/⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩\langle\phi|\psi\rangle/\langle\phi|\phi\rangle, as the average of the local matrices R⁡(S)R(S). Then [[⁡Ψ~|Φ​]]\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb is given as the average of R−1​(S)R^{-1}(S) either by sampling directly in terms of Ψ\Psi or in terms of Φ\Phi and importance weighting. Therefore, we can write:

[[⁡Φ~|Ψ​]]\displaystyle\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\Psi\rbb =𝔼S∼PΦ[R(S)],[[Ψ~|Φ]]=𝔼S∼PΨ[R−1(S)].\displaystyle=\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}[\,R(S)\,],\hskip 14.22636pt\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb=\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Psi}}[\,R^{-1}(S)\,]. (18)

The importance sampling expression becomes:

[[⁡Ψ~|Φ​]]=𝔼S∼PΦ⁡[|det⁡(R⁡(S))|2​R−1​(S)]𝔼S′∼PΦ⁡[|det⁡(R⁡(S′))|2],\lbb\widetilde{\Psi}|\Phi\rbb=\frac{\Ex_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\,|\det(R(S))|^{2}R^{-1}(S)\,\right]}{\Ex_{S^{\prime}\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[|\det(R(S^\prime))|^{2}\right]}, (19)

and equivalently for the other matrix.

The two fidelity matrices can then be estimated by multiplying the respective sampling expressions for the overlap matrices. This is the matrix analog of writing the standard VMC expression for the fidelity ℱ=|𝔼⁡[r⁡(s)]|2/𝔼⁡[|r⁡(s′)|2]\mathcal{F}=|\Ex[r(s)]|^{2}/\Ex[|r(s^{\prime})|^{2}] as the multiplication of ⟨ϕ|ψ⟩/⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩\langle\phi|\psi\rangle/\langle\phi|\phi\rangle as 𝔼⁡[r⁡(s)]\Ex[r(s)] by ⟨ψ|ϕ⟩/⟨ψ|ψ⟩\langle\psi|\phi\rangle/\langle\psi|\psi\rangle using importance sampling as 𝔼⁡[|r⁡(s)|2​r−1]​(s)/𝔼⁡[|r⁡(s′)|2]\Ex[|r(s)|^{2\,}r^{-1}](s)/\Ex[|r(s^{\prime})|^{2}]. Alternatively, a different sampling expression for the fidelity matrix F⁡(Φ|Ψ)F(\Phi|\Psi) can be obtained that does not require importance sampling. This is formulated as the matrix analog of the standard VMC formulation, rearranged as an estimator of ℱ−1−1\mathcal{F}^{-1}-1. For the scalar case, this becomes Var⁡[r⁡(s)/𝔼⁡[r⁡(s′)]]\Var[\,r(s)/\Ex[r(s^{\prime})]\,], and for the matrix case this becomes a wholly different sampling expression for F−1​(Φ|Ψ)−1F^{-1}(\Phi|\Psi)-1. Firstly, the normalization by the averages is given as Γ⁡(S)=R⁡(S)⋅(𝔼⁡[R⁡(S′)])−1\Gamma(S)=R(S)\cdot\left(\Ex[R(S^{\prime})]\right)^{-1}. Then the “variance” of the normalized local matrices Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S) is given identically as for OVMs and local operator matrices Eq. 14, where the covariance matrix of the local matrices’ total traces with their individual matrix elements is the general local matrix analog of the variance of scalar local values:

F−1​(Φ|Ψ)−1=CovS∼PΦ⁡[Tr⁡(Γ⁡(S)),Γ⁡(S)].\displaystyle F^{-1}(\Phi|\Psi)-1=\Cov_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\,\Tr( \Gamma(S) )\,,\,\Gamma(S)\,\right]. (20)

III.3.3 Metric Angle and Scalar Fidelity

Grassmann metrics can be defined analogously to the Fubini-Study metric for rays as sign-less angles between linear subspaces. The metric angles are constructed naturally as some averages of the individual principal angles, as Fubini-Study metric angle themselves. However, as there are many choices of average, there is no singular definition of a Grassmann metric angle and many definitions can be found in the math literature. Deriving a metric angle α\alpha, or equivalently a scalar fidelity as cos2⁡(α)\cos^{2}(\alpha), from the various Grassmann representations will also give different definitions depending on the chosen representation.

All the relevant definitions can be expressed as different generalized/power means of cos⁡(αi)\cos(\alpha_i). Fortunately, as we will show in the next section, these will give the same metric tensor. We denote the metric angle for the power mean pp-mean as α(p)​(𝒱,𝒱′)\alpha^{(p)}(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{V}^{\prime}) so that

cos⁡(α(p))=(1N​∑i=1Ncosp⁡(αi))1/p.\cos\small(\alpha^{(p)}\small)=\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\cos^{p}(\alpha_{i})\right)^{1/p}. (21)

The corresponding scalar pp-fidelity given as cos2⁡(α(p))\cos^{2}(\alpha^{(p)}), is equivalent to the p/2p/2-mean of the principal fidelities. This can be expressed in terms of fidelity matrices for any two bases Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V} and Ψ\Psi of 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime} as

ℱ(p)​(Φ,Ψ)=(1N​Tr⁡[Fp2​(Φ|Ψ)])2p.\mathcal{F}^{(p)}(\Phi,\Psi)=\left(\frac{1}{N}\Tr\left[F^{\frac{p}{2}}(\Phi|\Psi)\right]\right)^{\frac{2}{p}}. (22)

The power pp parameterizes the relative weighting of the principal angles/fidelities such that as pp increases more weight is given to the smaller angles/larger fidelities. p=1p=1 is the “Goldilocks” weighting, which gives the ideal gradient as individual Fubini-Study gradients concatenated in the principal bases. The power means p=0,1,2p=0,1,2 can each be related to the Grassmann representations. In particular, we have:

  • •

    00-Fidelity (Geometric Mean): Wedge-Product Representation. The pure state fidelity between the two wedge product states |Φ⟩⟩∧|\Phi\rwa and |Ψ⟩⟩∧|\Psi\rwa is given by the determinant of either fidelity matrix and ℱ(0)​(Φ,Ψ)\mathcal{F}^{(0)}(\Phi,\Psi) is the NN-th root of the determinant.

  • •

    11-Fidelity (Arithmetic Mean): Density Operator Representation. The mixed state fidelity between the density operators (Tr⁡ρ^𝒱⋅ρ^𝒱′)2\left(\Tr\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}}\cdot\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{V}^{\prime}}}\right)^{2} is equal to ℱ(1)​(Φ,Ψ)\mathcal{F}^{(1)}(\Phi,\Psi).

  • •

    22-Fidelity (Root Mean Square): Projector Representation. The Frobenius inner product between the orthogonal projectors Tr⁡(P^𝒱​P^𝒱′)\Tr\small(\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V^{\prime}}}\small) is proportional by 1/N1/N to ℱ(2)​(Φ,Ψ)\mathcal{F}^{(2)}(\Phi,\Psi) .

III.3.4 Metric Tensor and Tangent Spaces

Though there are multiple definitions of Grassmann metric angles, there is a singular standard definition of the Grassmann metric tensor which is ubiquitous in the literature. This is because the infinitesimal form metric angles α(p)\alpha^{(p)}, from which the corresponding metric tensor is derived, reduce to the same values for all powers pp. As a result, there is no ambiguity in defining tangent space quantities such as gradients and projections.

Formally, a metric tensor is defined from an inner product between pairs of tangent space vectors, so that the corresponding vector norm relates to the infinitesimal form of the metric. Grassmann tangent space vectors can be expressed (not uniquely) in a basis representation Φ\Phi as NN-tuples δ​Φ\delta\Phi of individual basis state perturbations. The induced norm ‖δ​Φ‖Φ=⟨δ​Φ,δ​Φ⟩Φ|\!|\delta\Phi|\!|_{\Phi}=\sqrt{\langle\delta\Phi,\delta\Phi\rangle_{\Phi}} on these perturbations is given so that (α(p)​(Φ,Φ+δ​Φ))2=‖δ​Φ‖Φ2+𝒪⁡(‖δ​Φ‖Φ4)\left(\alpha^{(p)}(\Phi,\Phi+\delta\Phi)\right)^{2}=|\!|\delta\Phi|\!|_{\Phi}^{2}+\mathcal{O}(|\!|\delta\Phi|\!|_{\Phi}^{4}) and is again independent of the power pp. The general form of the metric tensor as inner product between any pair of basis perturbations can be expressed compactly in the matrix representation as

⟨δ​Φ,δ​Φ′⟩Φ=1N​Tr⁡(G−1​(Φ)⋅[[⁡δ​Φ​|P^𝒱⟂|​δ​Φ′​]]).\langle\delta\Phi,\delta\Phi^{\prime}\rangle_{\Phi}=\frac{1}{N}\Tr\left(G^{-1}(\Phi)\cdot\lbb\delta\Phi|\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\delta\Phi^{\prime}\rbb\right). (23)

Functionally, the Grassmann metric tensor is a matrix promotion of the Fubini-Study metric tensor and can be derived equivalently using the previous techniques for operator values and fidelity. Similarly, it can also be derived as the Fubini-Study metric tensor in the wedge product representation, but again without the proportionality factor of 1/N1/N. This factor is also often not included in definitions found in the math literature, but we opt to keep it as it normalizes the inner products to be independent of the dimension and aligns with previous definitions for scalar operator values.

The abstract changes of directions of linear subspaces, which form the Grassmann tangent space 𝒯𝒱​𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}), can be expressed in the basis representation as perturbations δ​Φ\delta\Phi to the given basis Φ\Phi of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. However, this representation is not unique as different basis perturbations can result in the same linear subspace to first order. In order to define a bijective representation, the components of the basis perturbation that correspond to a change of equivalent basis as |δΦ]]=|Φ]]⋅δX|\delta\Phi\rbb=|\Phi\rbb\cdot\delta X for any δ​X∈G​LN​(ℂ)\delta X\in GL_{N}(\mathbb{C}) must be removed. This equivalently enforces that each individual basis state perturbation |δ​ϕi⟩|\delta\phi_{i}\rangle is orthogonal to 𝒱\mathcal{V} and thus 𝒯𝒱​𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)≃(𝒱⟂)N\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H})\simeq(\mathcal{V}^{\perp})^{N}. In the matrix representation, the tangent space ket matrices formed so that all their column vectors are in 𝒱⟂\mathcal{V}^{\perp} are given collectively as 𝒯𝒱​𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)≃{|δ​Φ​]]|​[[⁡Φ~|δ​Φ​]]=𝟎}\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H})\simeq\{|\delta\Phi\rbb\,|\,\lbb\widetilde{\Phi}|\delta\Phi\rbb=\boldsymbol{0}\}, where 𝟎\boldsymbol{0} indicates the matrix with zero entries. This is a higher-dimensional analog of the usual tangent space representation of the projective Hilbert space 𝒫⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H}), where the tangent space of a ray, represented by a given state ϕ\phi, is expressed bijectively as ℋϕ⟂\mathcal{H}_{\phi^{\perp}} [28]. In the wedge product representation, the tangent space vectors are given bijectively as |δ​ϕ1⟩∧|ϕ2⟩∧…∧|ϕN⟩+|ϕ1⟩∧|δ​ϕ2⟩∧…∧|ϕN⟩+…+|ϕ1⟩∧|ϕ2⟩∧…∧|δ​ϕN⟩|\delta\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge|\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge|\phi_{N}\rangle+|\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge|\delta\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge|\phi_{N}\rangle+\ldots+|\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge|\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge|\delta\phi_{N}\rangle.

IV Variational Grassmanians

In this section, we develop the framework for the variational representation of Grassmannians, extending the optimization of a single variational wave function to the simultaneous optimization of multiple ones.

IV.1 Constructing Variational Linear Subspaces

We will assume a variational construction of linear subspaces by the span of NN individual variational wave functions (VWFs) with an assumed linear independence. The variational linear subspace 𝒱⁡(θ)=span⁡(Φ⁡(θ))\mathcal{V}(\theta)=\spn(\Phi(\theta)) is then parametrized by the combined MM VWF weights θ=(θ1,…,θM)\theta=(\theta^{1},\ldots,\theta^{M}), which are assumed to be real and differentiable or complex and holomorphic. We will not assume whether each individual weight θμ\theta^{\mu} is unique to a specific VWF or shared between multiple VWFs, as there are advantages and disadvantages to both constructions. We consider the VWFs to be represented by neural quantum states (NQS) wave functions [7]. A NQS basis given by NN networks with identical architectures and separate sets of M/NM/N individual weights has ideal variational properties and gives block diagonal Jacobians. However, as the calculation of a single overlap matrix Φ⁡(S)=[[⁡S|Φ​]]\Phi(S)=\lbb S|\Phi\rbb requires N2N^{2} forward passes, then the computational cost of a VMC calculation with deep neural networks (DNNs) ansätze can be prohibitive for high-dimensional subspace. The overhead can be significantly reduced by sharing weights among the models. For instance, we can consider a NQS basis given collectively by a single shared DNN base — acting as a common backflow transformation [29] — paired with NN individual shallow neural network (SNN) heads. In this case, evaluating Φ⁡(S)\Phi(S) requires only NN DNN and N2N^{2} SNN forward passes, substantially lowering the total cost. This is precisely the architecture we decided to adopt in our simulations (see Section V).

IV.2 The Variational Manifold

Most standard VMC schemes for a single VWF ϕ⁡(θ)\phi(\theta), such as the Stochastic Reconfiguration method [26], can be formulated in terms of the differential geometry of the variational manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} [28], where ℳ⊂𝒫⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H}) formed as the sub manifold of the projective Hilbert space given by all the corresponding rays containing each possible VWF ϕ⁡(θ)\phi(\theta). The VWF weights θ\theta are then viewed as a working set of coordinates for ℳ\mathcal{M}. Variational problems are thus formulated in purely geometric terms, as the search for an optimal ray constrained to the variational manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. The VWF optimal weights are then given just as the coordinates of the ray solution. Using this geometric formulation, standard single VWF VMC methods can be generalized to multiple VWFs by fundamentally replacing projective geometry with Grassmann geometry. The Grassmann variational manifold ℳ⊂𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) is given analogously as the set of all the possible variational linear subspaces. Constructed from a VWF bases as 𝒱⁡(θ)=span⁡(Φ⁡(θ))\mathcal{V}(\theta)=\spn(\Phi(\theta)), the collective VWF weights θ\theta parameterize ℳ\mathcal{M} as a set of coordinates.

IV.3 Variational Tangent Spaces

The variational tangent space 𝒯𝒱⁡(θ)​ℳ\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}\mathcal{M} at each 𝒱⁡(θ)\mathcal{V}(\theta) is given by projecting the larger Grassmann tangent space 𝒯𝒱⁡(θ)​𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) to only directions which stay in the variational manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. These directions, as first order changes to 𝒱⁡(θ)\mathcal{V}(\theta), are all given uniquely by a corresponding perturbation in the VWF weights δ​θ\delta\theta and the resulting first order changes to the VWF basis ϕi​(θ+δ​θ)−ϕi​(θ)=δ​θμ​∂μϕi​(θ)+𝒪⁡(δ​θ2)\phi_{i}(\theta+\delta\theta)-\phi_{i}(\theta)=\delta\theta^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\phi_{i}(\theta)+\mathcal{O}(\delta\theta^{2}). The variational tangent vectors are then given by the spans of the coordinate basis vectors formed individually by the partial derivatives for each θμ\theta^{\mu}. However, as the Grassmann tangent space is bijectively represented by only basis perturbations which are orthogonal to 𝒱⁡(θ)\mathcal{V}(\theta), the components of the partial derivatives parallel to 𝒱⁡(θ)\mathcal{V}(\theta) must be projected out. In the matrix representation, the effective coordinate basis is then given as

𝒯𝒱⁡(θ)ℳ≃span{|Θμ(θ)]]=P^𝒱⟂|∂μΦ(θ)]]}μ.\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}\mathcal{M}\simeq\spn\left\{\,|\Theta_{\mu}(\theta)\rbb=\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\Phi(\theta)\rbb\,\right\}_{\mu}. (24)

This coordinate basis formulation is again just the matrix analog of the standard single state formulation [28], where the effective projective coordinate basis vectors are given by the states P^ϕ⟂​|∂μϕ⟩\hat{P}_{\phi^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\phi\rangle. In the wedge product representation, the effective Grassmann coordinate basis vectors is then P^∧iϕi⟂|∂μΦ⟩⟩∧=P^𝒱⟂|∂μϕ1⟩∧|ϕ2⟩∧…∧|ϕN⟩+|ϕ1⟩∧P^𝒱⟂|∂μϕ2⟩∧…∧|ϕN⟩+⋯+|ϕ1⟩∧|ϕ2⟩∧…∧P^𝒱⟂|∂μϕN⟩\hat{P}_{\wedge_{i}\phi_{i}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\Phi\rwa=\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge|\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge|\phi_{N}\rangle+|\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge|\phi_{N}\rangle+\dots+|\phi_{1}\rangle\wedge|\phi_{2}\rangle\wedge\ldots\wedge\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\mu}\phi_{N}\rangle.

IV.4 Quantum Geometric Tensor

The most straightforward geometric definition of the Quantum Geometric Tensor (QGT) [30, 31, 28] is as the induced metric tensor on the variational manifold. While for the single state it is induced by the Fubini-Study metric, the Grassmann QGT is then naturally induced from the Grassmann metric Eq. 23. The QGT matrix elements Sμ​ν\QGT_{\mu\nu} are given by the inner products of the corresponding coordinate basis pairs Θμ\Theta_{\mu} and Θν\Theta_{\nu}. This allows the inner product Eq. 23, restricted to pairs of variational tangent space vectors |U]]=Uμ|Θμ]]|U\rbb=U^{\mu}|\Theta_{\mu}\rbb and |W]]=Wν|Θν]]|W\rbb=W^{\nu}|\Theta_{\nu}\rbb to be expressed as Sμ​ν⁡U¯μ​Wν\QGT_{\mu\nu}\overline{U}^{\mu}W^{\nu}. For complex weights and holomorphic VWFs, the Grassmann QGT is given as the Hermitian positive definite matrix

Sμ​ν=1N​Tr⁡(G−1​[[​∂μΦ​|P^𝒱⟂|​∂νΦ​]]).\QGT_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{N}\Tr\left(G^{-1}\lbb\partial_{\mu}\Phi|\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}|\partial_{\nu}\Phi\rbb\right). (25)

For real parameters, only the real part of Eq. 25 must be taken, which gives a symmetric positive definite matrix.

Another interpretation of the QGT, which is practically important for VMC estimations, is as the covariance matrix of the partial derivatives. The Grassmann QGT maintains this relationship in terms of the previously defined Grassmann operator covariance, so that Sμ​ν(θ)=Cov𝒱⁡(θ)[∂μ,∂ν]\QGT_{\mu\nu}(\theta)=\Cov_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}[\partial_{\mu},\partial_{\nu}]. Defining D~μ​(S)=Φ−1​(S)⋅∂μΦ⁡(S)\widetilde{D}_{\mu}(S)=\Phi^{-1}(S)\cdot\partial_{\mu}\Phi(S) and using the same sampling formulation for operator covariances, the QGT matrix elements can be calculated as

Sμ​ν=1N​CovS∼PΦ⁡[Tr⁡(D~μ​(S)),Tr⁡(D~ν​(S))].\QGT_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{N}\Cov_{S\sim P_{\Phi}}\left[\,\Tr(\widetilde{D}_\mu(S))\,,\,\Tr(\widetilde{D}_\nu(S))\,\right]. (26)

This sampling expression is equivalent to the standard VMC one in the wedge product representation, as Tr⁡[D~μ​(S)]=∂μlog⁡(⟨⟨⁡S|Φ​⟩⟩∧)\Tr[\widetilde{D}_{\mu}(S)]=\partial_{\mu}\log( \lwa S | \Phi\rwa)S|\Phi\rwa. This follows from the overlap-determinant relation ⟨⟨⁡S|Φ​⟩⟩∧∝det⁡[Φ⁡(S)]\lwa S|\Phi\rwa\propto\det[\Phi(S)] and from the formula for the derivatives of the determinant ∂μlog⁡(det⁡[Φ⁡(S)])=Tr⁡[Φ−1​(S)⋅∂μΦ⁡(S)]\partial_{\mu}\log( \det[\Phi(S)] )=\Tr[\Phi^{-1}(S)\cdot\partial_{\mu}\Phi(S)].

IV.5 Optimization of Multiple Wave Functions and Stochastic Reconfiguration

The extension of the optimization through Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR) [26] to linear subspaces is straightforward using this geometric formalism. Loss functions ℒ\mathcal{L}, originally defined over individual wave functions, are now formulated over bases, Φ→ℒ⁡(Φ)\Phi\rightarrow\mathcal{L}(\Phi), and must remain invariant under changes of basis to be well-defined on linear subspaces. For VWF bases, the composite mapping gives the loss as a function over VWF weights: θ→ℒ⁡(Φ⁡(θ))\theta\rightarrow\mathcal{L}(\Phi(\theta)). The SR weight update Δ​θ\Delta\theta in the Grassmann setting is given identically as for standard SR as the solution of the following equations:

Sμ​ν⁡(θ)​Δ​θν=−η​∂ℒ∂θ¯μ​(Φ⁡(θ)),\QGT_{\mu\nu}(\theta)\,\Delta\theta^{\nu}=-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\overline{\theta}^{\mu}}(\Phi(\theta)), (27)

where η\eta denotes the step size or learning rate. This expression corresponds to natural gradient descent, where the QGT plays the role of the metric tensor, and the update follows the gradient adapted to the geometry of the variational manifold. In terms of tangent vectors in the matrix representation, the gradient of ℒ\mathcal{L} defined over the variational manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} is |ℒℳ/δΦ]]=(S−1)μ​ν∂νℒ|Θμ]]|\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{M}}/\delta\Phi\rbb=(\QGT^{-1})^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\nu}\mathcal{L}\,|\Theta_{\mu}\rbb.

More generally, SR can also be viewed as approximating some target evolution while being constrained to the variational manifold. In the continuous-time setting, the approximate velocity at each time is given by projecting the target velocity onto the variational manifold. For loss minimization, the target evolution is the unconstrained gradient descent direction |δℒ/δΦ]]|\delta\mathcal{L}/\delta\Phi\rbb defined over the full Grassmann manifold 𝐆𝐫N​(ℋ)\mathbf{Gr}_{N}(\mathcal{H}). Projecting this onto ℳ\mathcal{M} yields the gradient restricted to the variational submanifold. The projected Grassmann tangent space where the variational velocity is given by

𝒫𝒯𝒱⁡(θ)​ℳ(|W]])=|Θμ]](S−1(θ))μ​ν⟨Θν,W⟩𝒱⁡(θ).\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}\mathcal{M}}(|W\rbb)=|\Theta_{\mu}\rbb(\QGT^{-1}(\theta))^{\mu\nu}\,\langle\Theta_{\nu},W\,\rangle_{\mathcal{V}(\theta)}. (28)

V Results

To test the efficacy of the Grassmann VMC framework formalized in the previous sections, we apply it to find the excited states of a quantum spin Hamiltonian, in the same fashion as done in [1] for continuous-space systems. Let us consider an Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} of a system of NsN_{s} spins-12\frac{1}{2} with basis states {|s⟩}={|s1,…,sNs⟩}\{\ket*{s}\}=\{\ket*{s^1, \ldots, s^{N_s}}\}, where si=±1s^{i}=\pm 1 for i=1,…,Nsi=1,\ldots,N_{s}. We focus on a two-dimensional spin lattice such that Ns=L×LN_{s}=L\times L, where LL is the linear dimension of the lattice. The basis wave functions ϕi\phi_{i} are parametrized as neural wave functions with the following architecture:

ϕi​(s)=fθi​(CNNΘ​(s)),\phi_{i}(s)=f_{\theta_{i}}(\text{CNN}_{\Theta}(s)), (29)

where θi\theta_{i} and Θ\Theta are real parameters. The internal CNN corresponds to a real-valued convolutional neural network inspired by the ConvNeXt architecture [32, 33], already employed in the context of ground state search [34, 35]. Given an input spin configuration s∈[−1,1]L×Ls\in[-1,1]^{L\times L} the network begins with a convolutional layer using a filter of size K×KK\times K, unit stride, and periodic boundary conditions, producing a feature map y∈ℝL×L×Cy\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times C}, where CC denotes the number of channels. The network then processes this feature map through GG stages. Each stage first applies a dense layer projecting the input to w∈ℝL×L×dw\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times d}, followed by a sequence of BB residual blocks. For each block, denoting its input as xinx_{\text{in}}, the following operations are performed in order:

  • •

    depth-wise convolution with Kd​w×Kd​wK_{dw}\times K_{dw} filter xin→x(1)∈ℝL×L×dx_{\text{in}}\to x^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times d},

  • •

    layer normalization [36],

  • •

    dense layer x(1)→x(2)∈ℝL×L×(f⋅d)x^{(1)}\to x^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times(f\cdot d)} realizing the inverted bottleneck with expansion ratio ff,

  • •

    GELU activation function,

  • •

    global response normalization [33]

  • •

    dense layer x(2)→x(3)∈ℝL×L×dx^{(2)}\to x^{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times d},

  • •

    rescaling x(4)=γ⋅x(3)x^{(4)}=\gamma\cdot x^{(3)} where γ\gamma is a learnable parameter,

  • •

    residual connection xout=xin+x(4)x_{\text{out}}=x_{\text{in}}+x^{(4)}.

The final output of all the stages z∈ℝL×L×dz\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times d} is then subjected to a last layer normalization, flattened and given as input to the fθif_{\theta_{i}} which correspond to complex-valued Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) [7]. The CNN acts as a common backflow transformation of the spin coordinates which is shared by all the ansätze, while the RBMs are specific for each variational wave function. This approach is in line with the representational learning paradigm [37] already employed in previous works on ground state [10, 38]. The CNN model is equivariant with respect to translational and spin-flip symmetries of the input, while the RBMs implement momentum and spin projection, making the final wave functions invariant under these symmetries. The ansätze are optimized using the SR method for Grassmannians formalized in the previous section. Similarly to the single-state case, we also leverage the Woodbury matrix identity to speed up SR updates in the limit of number of samples much smaller than the number of variational parameters [11, 39]. The sampling is restricted to the sector with zero total zz-magnetization. The Marshall sign-rule [40] is applied to the outputs of the neural networks.

The quantum spin system we investigate is the paradigmatic antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model in two dimensions, whose Hamiltonian is:

H^=∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j,\hat{H}=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j}, (30)

where 𝑺^i=(S^ix,S^iy,S^iz)\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}=(\hat{S}_{i}^{x},\hat{S}_{i}^{y},\hat{S}_{i}^{z}) is the spin-12\frac{1}{2} operator at site ii and the sum runs over all the nearest-neighboring sites. We consider square lattice geometries with periodic boundary conditions along both spatial directions.

First, we benchmark on a 6×66\times 6 system, where exact diagonalization (ED) is still attainable. Besides the energies of the excited states, we also compute the spin structure factor:

S(𝒌)=⟨S^𝒌†S^𝒌⟩withS^𝒌=1N∑𝒍e−i𝒌⋅𝒍S^𝒍z,S(\boldsymbol{k})=\langle\hat{S}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hat{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle\,\,\text{with}\,\,\hat{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{l}}e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}}\hat{S}_{\boldsymbol{l}}^{z}, (31)

where the vector 𝒍\boldsymbol{l} gives the position of the sites in the lattice. Due to the enforcement of both zero total zz-magnetization and translational symmetry in the ansätze, the spin structure factor is equivalently the expectation of S^𝒌†​P^𝒱⟂​S^𝒌\hat{S}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}\hat{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}} for each of the basis wave functions that span 𝒱\mathcal{V}. We then obtain the spin structure factor values from the diagonals of the OVM for S^𝒌\hat{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}.

In Fig. 2, we show the comparison between our results and the ED benchmark for the first 4 excited states in different momentum sectors. The results demonstrate remarkable accuracy in both the energy and the structure factor S⁡(π,π)S(\pi,\pi), across all excitations and momentum sectors. As shown in the inset, the relative energy errors remain consistently below or around 10−410^{-4} across the spectrum. We observe that the discrepancies become more pronounced for higher excited states, in line with the findings of [1].

After benchmarking, we investigate a larger 10×1010\times 10 lattice. The corresponding 6 excited-state energies are shown in Fig. 3. The V-scores [42] values reported in the inset validate the accuracy of the variational results, remaining of the order of 10−310^{-3} or below across all excited states and momentum sectors. We remark that for a given V-score the actual energy relative error is typically an order of magnitude smaller [42]. For the ground state in the 𝒒=Γ\boldsymbol{q}=\Gamma sector, we also report the Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) estimate for the energy [41], EQMC/Ns=−0.671549​(4)E_{\text{QMC}}/N_{s}=-0.671549(4), which is in excellent agreement with our result E/Ns=−0.671544​(4)E/N_{s}=-0.671544(4). Finally, in Fig. 4, we present three-dimensional plots of the spin structure factor in the 𝒒=Γ\boldsymbol{q}=\Gamma momentum sector. In all the cases, the peak occurs at 𝒌=(π,π)\boldsymbol{k}=(\pi,\pi), though with varying intensity across different excited states. The peak value S​(π,π)=5.35​(9)S(\pi,\pi)=5.35(9) for the ground state agrees with the QMC result SQMC​(π,π)=5.3124​(3)S_{\text{QMC}}(\pi,\pi)=5.3124(3) [41].

For the simulations, we considered the following network hyperparameters: G=3G=3 stages with B=2,2,8B=2,2,8 number of blocks, d=4,6,12d=4,6,12 for the 6×66\times 6 and d=8,12,20d=8,12,20 for the 10×1010\times 10, C=4C=4 for the 6×66\times 6 and C=6C=6 for the 10×1010\times 10. The filter sizes are set to K=3K=3 and Kd​w=5K_{dw}=5, and the expansion ratio to f=4f=4. For the RBMs, we employed 16 hidden units for the 6×66\times 6 and 12 for the 10×1010\times 10. We typically use 2112^{11} Monte Carlo samples and perform around 50005000 SR steps with a learning rate of η=0.15/Ns\eta=0.15/N_{s}. The QGT inversion is stabilized with a diagonal shift of 10−310^{-3}. Finally, parameter updates are performed using the SPRING algorithm [43].

VI Conclusions

We presented a rigorous geometric formulation of the variational principle for excited states introduced in [1] in terms of Grassmannians in the Hilbert space. This enables the generalization of the Stochastic Reconfiguration method and the introduction of the multidimensional extensions of operator variances and subspace overlaps. We apply the framework to investigate the properties of excited states in the 2D antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, achieving accurate excitation energies and capturing key physical observables across a large portion of the spectrum. The approach overcomes limitations of prior methods — such as instability in dense spectra and reliance on symmetry constraints — without introducing additional penalty terms or fine-tuned hyperparameters. Possible future directions include the application of the framework to lattice fermions and frustrated spin systems. The generalization of the overlap to multiple wave functions opens interesting venues such as the simulation of real-time dynamics through subspace expansion methods [44, 21] and schemes based on infidelity minimization [45, 46, 47, 48, 19, 49]. Potential future applications include integrating the method with quantum hardware through hybrid optimization.

VII Software

All the simulations have been carried out using the software package NetKet [50, 51]. The code will be made public in a later revision of the manuscript. We acknowledge the use of SpinED [52] for the exact benchmarks.
